strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP need: compact generative models for ten Indian languages, including several underserved languages. The reported 13–368M parameter sizes and emphasis on CPU inference target practical deployment constraints.

Some reported instruction-tuning gains are promising. For example, Hindi Belebele accuracy increases from 23.33% to 42.78%, and Bangla Belebele accuracy increases from 25.11% to 32.45%. These results suggest useful task adaptation at modest model sizes.

The evaluation includes established multilingual benchmarks, native-speaker assessments, and numerous concrete prompts and outputs. Reporting training-token counts, GPU hours, and inference speeds provides useful information, although the experimental specification remains incomplete.
weaknesses: The central RoPE memory-saving claim is unsupported. The paper describes a scaling ratio but provides neither a precise algorithm nor controlled memory measurements. Rescaling positional coordinates alone does not reduce the attention and activation memory associated with processing a fixed number of tokens. The distinction between training on shorter sequences and actually training with a longer context is unresolved. An explicit implementation and comparisons against standard RoPE and positional interpolation are necessary.

Reproducibility is substantially inadequate. Essential architecture and optimization details, corpus sources and unique sizes, language-mixture proportions, and checkpoint-selection procedures are missing. No implementation/checkpoint access or sufficiently complete reconstruction recipe is supplied. Evaluation templates and context-truncation procedures are also unspecified; these matter particularly for 25-shot evaluation with a 1024-token context. Table 18 omits the CPU model, thread count, and sequence lengths needed to reproduce its inference measurements.

The human evaluation cannot support the broad generation-superiority claims. It uses only four prompts per evaluated language, generally with three outputs per prompt, and does not report per-language annotator counts, blinding, agreement, or uncertainty. Literary prompts require overlap checks against the curated training books. Assigning factuality zero when a claim cannot be verified conflates unverifiability with falsehood. The October 2023 ChatGPT website comparison does not establish equivalent decoding controls, and many other baselines predominantly target English. A larger, representative, blinded evaluation is needed.

The quantitative results do not establish the claimed effective transfer or avoidance of the curse of multilinguality. For example, mParamanu achieves 24.84% on Hindi MMLU and 25.68% on Marathi MMLU, approximately the 25% random-choice baseline. Its Hindi XNLI result, 33.70%, is likewise near the three-class chance level. No confidence intervals or controlled ablations isolate script grouping and corpus balancing from differences in training data, language coverage, and model capacity. The genuine-looking instruction-tuning improvements do not validate these separate causal claims.

The tokenizer contribution is insufficiently specified and evaluated. Figure 3 does not explain how BPE and Unigram models, vocabularies, or merge rules are combined. The fertility comparison lacks a clearly documented common evaluation corpus and vocabulary-budget comparison. Moreover, Table 3's per-token perplexities are not directly comparable across different languages and tokenizers; this undermines both the tokenizer comparison and the interpretation of Sanskrit versus Hindi perplexity. Comparisons on common held-out text using comparable units, plus downstream ablations, are needed.

Material reporting inconsistencies reduce confidence in the results. In Table 7, the six Hindi instruction-model scores average to 38.49%, not the reported 40.14%. Instruction-tuning data are variously described as 23,000 examples, 27,000 examples, and—for Hindi—27,000 plus 52,000 Alpaca examples. Table 12 describes both top-three and top-five generations and uses inconsistent evaluation labels. These issues require a systematic audit. Together with the missing methods and insufficient validation, they warrant substantial methodological and experimental work before the paper meets Findings' soundness and reproducibility threshold.
